UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

     RWE AMERICAS, LLC                                )
                                                      )
        Complainant                                   )            Docket No. EL26-106-000
                                                      )

     PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                      )

        Respondent                                    )

    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF RWE AMERICAS, LLC

        The Commission must decide each individual Complaint on the facts that are presented.

Here, RWE provided a wealth of evidence which demonstrated that, for the five Projects at issue,

(i) RWE satisfied the PJM Tariff and Manual requirements and answered and cured the items PJM

raised in the Deficiency Notices, (ii) PJM mismanaged its review causing confusion by raising

deficiency claims that were inconsistent with, or not rooted in, its Tariff or Manuals, or (iii) PJM

applied inconsistent application of its modeling standards as clearly shown by comparison to the

16 RWE projects that PJM allowed to proceed in Cycle 01 for which RWE applied the same

methodology, resulting in PJM violating the no undue discrimination clause of the FPA. PJM’s

Answer 1 does not meaningfully rebut the facts and arguments RWE presented in the Complaint.2

Instead, PJM makes conclusory claims and fails to engage the Project-by-Project evidence that




1      RWE Americas, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No.
EL26-106-000 (Sep. 24, 2026) (“PJM Answer”).
2        RWE Americas, LLC v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Complaint and Requests for Fast Track Processing and
Shortened Answer Period of RWE Americas, LLC, Docket No. EL26-106-000 (Sep. 4, 2026) (“Complaint”).
Capitalized terms used herein but not defined herein have the meaning provided in the Complaint.
 RWE included with its Complaint.3 Further, PJM’s Answer confirms that it applied requirements

that are neither in the PJM Tariff nor its Manuals to remove Livingston Wind 24 from Cycle 01,

and PJM failed to provide that Project with the required 10-business-day period to cure new

“deficiencies” that PJM identified.

       PJM does not dispute RWE’s core position on the BESS Projects: PJM implemented its

deficiency review and cure procedures inconsistently across similarly-situated projects, extending

flexibility, clarification, and administrative accommodation to some projects, while withdrawing

comparable or better-documented projects. In Attachments P, Q, R, and S, RWE lists the modeling

issues that PJM identified for each BESS Project, cross-referencing Attachments K, L, M, and O

that show the “deficiencies” PJM flagged for each Project. Attachments P, Q, R, and S then

identify specific RWE projects that had substantially similar deficiencies and shows that PJM

treated the four BESS Projects at issue in this Complaint docket differently than other RWE

projects that PJM accepted into Cycle 01. This evidence is unambiguous and revealing, yet PJM

provides no substantive answer whatsoever.              This unrebutted evidence affirms that PJM

erroneously withdrew the four BESS Projects from Cycle 01. As shown Project-by-Project below,

PJM’s arguments cannot withstand scrutiny when measured against RWE’s factual cure record

and PJM’s own conduct with comparable projects. The unrebutted evidence compels only one

result: the four BESS Projects (C01-1680, C01-1681, C01-1687, and C01-1708) must be restored

to Cycle 01. Any other result will be contrary to substantial evidence in the record and the FPA

prohibition on undue discrimination requirement.




3      Project Identifier Nos. C01-1680, C01-1681, C01-1687, and C01-1708.
4      Project Identifier No. C01-1705.
                                                    2
        For Livingston Wind 2, PJM concedes “RWE is correct that the PJM’s Tariff and Manuals

do not impose an explicit bar on the same legal entity submitting two New Service Requests using

the same Site”.5 Instead, PJM introduces an entirely new theory to justify its withdrawal of

Livingston Wind 2 from Cycle 01: a single LLC cannot demonstrate site control “conveyance”

and “exclusivity” for two separate projects.6 This new argument is absurd. First, PJM provides

no Tariff or Manual citation to back its new theory as applied to a single entity with two requests;

nor could it in view of PJM’s concession that the same entity can submit two requests to use the

same site. Second, here, the same LLC owns both projects (Livingston Wind 1 (Project Identifier

No. C01-1704) and Livingston Wind 2), which was clear from their Cycle 01 applications and

confirmed during the deficiency cure period. The single LLC received conveyance and exclusivity

for the property from the landowners and identified the separate locations where each project will

be located. RWE provided this information to PJM, showing where each project is located on the

site. The information RWE provided meets all the site control requirements for each project.

There is nothing in the filed rate (PJM Tariff) that allows PJM to withdraw Livingston Wind 2 on

this new theory. Moreover, even if a new site control deficiency existed on this newly raised

conveyance and exclusivity theory, Tariff Section 403(B)(1)(b) requires that PJM inform the

customer of the deficiency and provide a 10-business-day cure period, which RWE never received.

PJM cannot simply withdraw applications for undisclosed deficiencies or after-the-fact

justifications. That is contrary to the Commission’s transparency principle underlying its open

access generation policies and the notice requirement of the filed rate doctrine.




5      PJM Answer at 20.
6      Id.
                                                 3
         Accordingly, for the reasons set forth below, RWE respectfully requests that the

Commission grant leave for RWE to file this Answer with its Attachments, find that PJM’s

withdrawal of the Projects from Cycle 01 was unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory in

violation of the FPA and the PJM Tariff, and direct PJM to reinstate the five Projects into Cycle 01

with their original queue positions.

I.      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Commission,7

RWE submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the PJM Answer. Although the

Commission’s regulations do not allow for an answer to an answer as of right, the Commission

accepts such answers when the information will assist the Commission in its decision-making

process by addressing relevant issues in the proceeding and facilitating the development of the

record.8 This Answer meets that standard. The PJM Answer advances new arguments and

rationales that were unknown until now. This Answer will assist the Commission’s decision-

making by addressing these new positions and correcting the record on a Project-by-Project basis.

Accordingly, RWE respectfully requests that the Commission grant RWE leave to file this Answer

and to accept it into the record.

II.     ANSWER
        A.       RWE Has Met Its Prima Facie Burden Under FPA Section 206, and PJM’s
                 Answer Does Not Rebut The Evidence That RWE Presented.

        As a threshold matter, the Commission should recognize that RWE has met its prima facie

burden under FPA Section 206. RWE’s Complaint identified independent violations of the Tariff


7       18 C.F.R. §§ 385.12, 385.213.
8         See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,084 at P 13 (2025) (accepting an answer to an answer
after finding it provided information that assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); ISO New England
Inc., 187 FERC ¶ 61,175 at P 14 (2024) (same); California Independent System Operator Corp., 179 FERC ¶ 61,151
at P 13 (2022) (same).
                                                         4
 and the FPA.9 A complainant satisfies its burden by clearly identifying the action or inaction

alleged to violate applicable statutory standards or regulatory requirements and explaining how

that action or inaction violates the standard.10 Here, RWE supported every claimed Tariff violation

and position with evidence. RWE summarized the evidence in the body of the Complaint and

included the actual evidence in the Attachments to the Complaint. Once RWE made that prima

facie showing, the burden shifted to PJM to rebut that evidence. Notwithstanding this evidentiary

showing, PJM argues that RWE has not met its FPA burden. 11 The record shows otherwise, and

the Commission should find that RWE has met its prima facie burden under FPA Section 206.

        Regarding the four BESS Projects, PJM principally responds that the Complaint offers only

“broad-brush” assertions and fails to identify unduly discriminatory treatment of the Projects.12

Indeed, PJM claims that RWE “declined to undertake” a “project-by-project” analysis in the

Complaint.13 This is patently incorrect. As shown on pages 5-10 and 12-14 of the Complaint, as

well as in Attachments K through M, O, and P through S, the Complaint shows, on a project-by-

project basis, each deficiency that PJM identified during the review process and each corrective

action RWE took in response during the cure period, and then demonstrates how PJM’s treatment

of the BESS Projects did not align with PJM’s treatment of the similarly-situated projects

identified in Attachments P through S that PJM allowed to move forward in Cycle 01. The PJM

Answer does not dispute or even respond to this wealth of project-by-project data and analysis.

Instead, it is PJM that makes a conclusory, “broad brush” answer that its conduct was not unduly


9       See, e.g., Complaint at 14-20.
10      See, e.g., City of Anaheim v. Trans Bay Cable L.L.C., 146 FERC ¶ 61,100, at n.25 (2014) (citing 18 C.F.R.
§ 385.206(b)(1)-(2)).
11      PJM Answer at 18.
12      Id. at 19.
13      Id.
                                                       5
 discriminatory, and PJM makes this assertion without any factual support or comparative analysis.

PJM ignores all the comparative evidence that RWE provided. This evidence plainly showed that

PJM applied different standards to similarly situated customers.

       PJM is grasping at straws to claim that the extensive data RWE presented in its Complaint

is not evidence.14    The importance of the data is unmistakable. To the extent PJM seeks

“sponsored” evidence, RWE attaches Attachment V as an affidavit that verifies those facts.15 This

affidavit only verifies the facts that RWE presented already. The affidavit does not add any

supplemental information or prejudice PJM in any way.

       The Complaint shows that PJM accepted 16 RWE projects that used the same technical

approach to resolve the same modeling deficiencies that PJM identified for the BESS Projects.

The PJM Answer does not provide any objective evidence or rationale that distinguishes the four

BESS Projects from the 16 accepted RWE applications. The FPA does not allow PJM to treat

such similarly-situated customers differently without a discernable, reasoned basis, and PJM’s

Answer supplies none and instead relies on a conclusory, “broad brush,” bald assertion that each

RWE cure response was simply technically deficient without any explanation or comparison

regarding the 16 projects PJM accepted into Cycle 01 that submitted the same technical

information as the four BESS Projects. Indeed, PJM has had the models and technical data to

challenge RWE’s position for months. If PJM possessed a genuine, articulable basis to distinguish

the four BESS Projects from the 16 accepted PJM applications, it would have stated that basis in




14     Id. at 2.
15     Affidavit of Kathik Mekala (Attachment V).
                                                    6
 its Answer; PJM did not. Assertions without evidentiary backing and analysis render PJM’s

Answer bald and inconsequential.16

        Regarding Livingston Wind 2, although PJM claims that “RWE failed to cure deficiencies

related to Site Control and was properly withdrawn,”17 RWE already provided evidence that it

resolved the site control issues PJM flagged in the deficiency notice.                      As documented in

Attachment N issue 4, PJM confirmed in the NextGen portal that RWE cured all site control

deficiencies and all other deficiencies. 18 However, after RWE cured all deficiencies, PJM asserted

a new deficiency that PJM used to withdraw this project from Cycle 01, claiming that separate

LLCs must own two projects on the same site and that those LLCs execute a Shared Facilities

Agreement.19 PJM offered no support for this claim, nor could it have because there is no such

provision in the PJM Tariff; as noted, PJM now admits “RWE is correct that the PJM’s Tariff and

Manuals do not impose an explicit bar on the same legal entity submitting two New Service

Requests using the same Site.”20 Thus, the basis that PJM used to withdraw this Project from

Cycle 01 PJM now concedes was erroneous. Indeed, PJM’s concession renders its claim that a

Shared Facilities Agreement was required an absurdity because the same single interconnection

customer cannot have a valid contract with itself.21 Further, even if providing a Shared Facilities

Agreement was a valid deficiency, PJM did not provide the 10-business-day cure period that Tariff

Section 403(B)(1)(b) requires after PJM first identifies the “deficiency.” PJM cannot identify a


16       California Independent System Operator Corporation, et al., 121 FERC ¶ 61,281 at P 52 (2007) (refusing to
accept a “bald assertion” in answer).

18      Attachment N (noting that the NextGen portal states the site control deficiency was cured by the deficiency
response)

 new claimed deficiency now and argue there is no opportunity to answer and cure. If there is no

opportunity to answer and cure, then likewise there can be no opportunity for PJM to raise a new

claimed deficiency.        Any other process does not strike the appropriate balance between

monopolistic transmission provider and customer.

       In sum, insofar as evidence is concerned, RWE made its prima facie showing for all five

Projects. Thereafter, the burden of production and rebuttal shifted to PJM. PJM’s Answer shows

it has not carried that burden.

       B.           PJM’s Project-Specific Rationales Do Not Justify Withdrawal Of Any Of The
                    Five Projects.

                    1.    C01-1680 (York River BESS 1)

       PJM states that the withdrawal of C01-1680 is principally due to RWE’s alleged failure to

cure deficiencies related to reactive power capability curve data, missing parameters in the

Dynamic Model Report, and missing information on the site plan.22            RWE disputes this

characterization.

       With regard to the site plan, PJM’s Deficiency Notice for C01-1680 requested that RWE

“Amend kmz to show boundaries for the generating facility, collector substation, and the location

of the POI at the existing Grafton substation.”23 PJM’s Withdrawal Notice stated that “Generating

Facilities not labeled by Project ID in kmz (C01-1680 and C01-1681); No gen tie path shown

between Collector Substation and POI.”24 In Attachment K, RWE showed how it resolved all the

deficiencies that PJM identified. In Attachment K, RWE explained it “[a]mended KMZ to show

boundary, collector sub, and the POI. Project boundaries are shown in the PDF site plan along with



22     Id. at 13.
23     Attachment A.
24     Attachment F.
                                                 8
 parcel IDs to show in the summary sheet and corresponding project.” PJM has provided no answer

to this evidence that addressed the deficiency point.

        Regarding the reactive power capability curve data and missing parameters in the Dynamic

Model Report, PJM identified other Cycle 01 projects in the same situation that provided the same

response.25 RWE engineers submitted the responses using the same methods to address these

issues for C01-1680 and the four projects identified in Attachment P (C01-1711, C01-1684, C01-

1702, C01-1704). PJM withdrew C01-1680 from Cycle 01, but PJM allowed the four projects

identified in Attachment P to continue in Cycle 01.26 PJM provides no answer to justify why it

did not apply the same treatment to C01-1680 as it applied to these similarly-situated projects.

                 2.       C01-1681 (York River BESS 2)

        PJM states that the withdrawal of C01-1681 is principally due to a mismatch between the

Dynamic Model Report and NextGen and a missing site plan boundary identification. 27 RWE

disputes this characterization.

        With regard to the site plan, PJM’s Deficiency Notice for York River BESS 2 requested

that RWE “Amend kmz to show boundaries for the generating facility, collector substation, and

the location of the POI at the existing Grafton substation.”28 PJM’s Withdrawal Notice stated,

“Generating Facilities not labeled by Project ID in kmz (C01-1680 and C01-1681); No gen tie path

shown between Collector Substation and POI.”29 In Attachment L, RWE showed how it resolved

all the identified deficiencies and explained that it “[a]mended KMZ to show boundary, collector

 sub, and the POI. Project boundaries are shown in the PDF site plan along with parcel IDs to show

       Regarding the reactive power capability curve data and missing parameters in the Dynamic

Model Report, in Attachment Q RWE identified other Cycle 01 projects (C01-1684 and C01-1704)

in the same situation that provided the same deficiency cure response to PJM, which PJM thereafter

deemed sufficient to cure the deficiencies for those two projects. RWE engineers used the same

methods to address these same issues for all three projects. PJM withdrew C01-1681 from Cycle

01, yet it allowed the projects identified in Attachment Q (C01-1684 and C01-1704) to continue

in Cycle 01 and provide additional information at DP1. PJM has provided no justification for why

it did not apply the same treatment to C01-1681 as it applied to these similarly-situated projects.

               3.      C01-1687 (Meade BESS)

       PJM states that the withdrawal of C01-1687 is principally due to mismatched data between

the load flow model and NextGen, use of an incorrect PSSE model version, and invalid power

factor assessment tests.30 RWE disputes this characterization.

       First, on the mismatched data, the correct data was listed in the models that RWE provided

and that PJM would use. After all, that is what PJM is supposed to do during the application

review process: demonstrate that the math supporting each Interconnection Request works. RWE

showed that it did. Yet, because of the cover sheet so to speak, PJM withdrew the project from

Cycle 01.    The point here is to ensure a sound project design, which RWE qualitatively

demonstrated. PJM’s decision to remove a project for a minor posting discrepancy is additionally

unjust and unreasonable in view of PJM’s pronounced need for new generation resources – fast.


30     PJM Answer at 14.
                                                10
 PJM’s implementation is further egregious in view of the fact the minor typographical error can

be corrected in minutes, as RWE explained and which PJM also does not rebut.

       Second, contrary to PJM’s assertion, neither the Deficiency Notice nor the Withdrawal

Notice for C01-1687 mentioned an incorrect PSSE model. 31 The PSSE model was not at issue.

PJM provides no evidence to support this new claim. Indeed, PJM does not identify what was

incorrect about the PSSE model, nor could it. RWE provided a proper PSSE model and used the

same PSSE model for all the requests it submitted in Cycle 01.

       The Withdrawal Notice stated only “Failed to meet Stability requirements. See comments

in NextGen.”32 In Attachment M, RWE showed how it cured every deficiency that PJM identified

in the Deficiency Notice. Further, in Attachment R, PJM identified four other RWE Cycle 01

projects (C01-1684, C01-1704, C01-1706, C01-1711) with the same modeling to address stability

deficiencies. RWE engineers used the same method and provided the same information to address

these modeling issues for projects C01-1684, C01-1704, C01-1706, C01-1711 as they did for

project C01-1687. PJM allowed the four projects to continue in Cycle 01. PJM withdrew project

C01-1687. PJM has provided no justification for why it did not apply the same treatment to C01-

1687 as it applied to these similarly-situated projects.

               4.      C01-1708 (Kendall County BESS)

       PJM states that the withdrawal of C01-1708 is principally due to modeling file errors and

power factor assessments performed outside the defined ranges of the reactive power capability

curve.33 RWE disputes this characterization.

32     Attachment H.

         In Attachment O, RWE shows how it cured all 17 deficiencies that PJM identified in its

Deficiency Notice, providing detailed, itemized corrections and calculations for each deficiency.

Further, in Attachment S, PJM identified other RWE Cycle 01 projects with the same reactive

power and modeling deficiencies. RWE engineers used the same methods and provided the same

data to address these issues for the 16 RWE projects identified in Attachment S as it did for project

C01-1708. PJM allowed the 16 projects identified in Attachment S to continue in Cycle 01 and

yet PJM withdrew project C01-1708. PJM has provided no justification for why it did not apply

the same treatment to C01-1708 as it applied to these 16 similarly-situated projects.

                 5.      C01-1705 (Livingston Wind 2)

        The application for C01-1705 listed the Project as a New Service Request, not an uprate.34

PJM does not refute this. In its Answer, PJM acknowledges that the standards for uprates are

different than the standards for New Service Requests.35 Although PJM has noted that the

information in the application must be correct because PJM will rely on this information “to

properly and efficiently evaluate numerous applications for a given Cycle,”36 PJM ignored the

C01-1705 application and mischaracterized the project as an uprate, which has created the

confusion.

        On June 5, 2026, PJM issued a Deficiency Notice, but it still treated C01-1705 as an uprate,

not a New Service Request.37 On June 20, 2026, RWE cured all five deficiencies that PJM

under the same legal entity using the same Site Control evidence, and requested two separate Generation
Interconnection Agreements”).
35      Id. at 11 (explaining that for uprate projects the DMDG requires Project Developers to submit a combined
dynamic model showing both the base and uprate projects).
36      PJM Answer at 10-11, 23 (citing DMDG Sections 5.2, 5.2.2.1, 10.5) (“data and information provided in the
[Data Application] form shall match the data and parameters provided as the model for the project.”)

 identified, including a site control deficiency, which PJM does not dispute.38 However, after RWE

cured all the deficiencies, PJM finally recognized that project C01-1705 is a New Service Request,

not an uprate. Thereafter, in a July 21, 2026, email39 and now again in its Answer, PJM has

attempted to impose new site control requirements on the project.

       First, in July, PJM stated that RWE must put project C01-1705 in a separate LLC from

C01-1704 for C01-1705 to be treated as a New Service Request. However, PJM has conceded that

this requirement is not supported by its Tariff or Manuals, which means the application was not

deficient on this claimed point.40

       Now, according to the PJM Answer, the site control is deficient because “a deed or lease

cannot convey an exclusive right to the same legal entity twice, nor can it show conveyance to the

same legal entity twice.”41 Here, a single LLC owns both projects, and PJM admits that the Tariff

and Manuals do not prohibit a single LLC from owning two separate new services requests at the

same site. The single LLC received an exclusive conveyance for all the rights, including the term,

that two projects (C01-1704 and C01-1705) require. PJM has not contested these facts because it

cannot. The PJM Tariff and Manuals do not require two conveyances because there is no need for

and cannot be two conveyances. Two conveyances would be nonsensical when the owner of the

projects already has all the site control required. In fact, PJM Manual 14H, Section 7.1.2 explains

that “if multiple New Service Requests plan to utilize the same Site, the Project Developer must

provide evidence that the total acreage amount of the Site is adequate to support all such related

39     See Attachment T.

41     Id.
                                                      13
 New Service Requests.” C01-1705 has done exactly that and satisfied its site control requirement.

Indeed, PJM does not show otherwise because it cannot.

         PJM also now states for that when there are two or more projects at the same site, the

Developer must show that each request is “concurrently feasible with the development of any other

projects that will share the Site identified in the Site Control.”42 RWE agrees, and RWE has shown

precisely that in its applications. PJM has never provided any basis for why the two projects (C01-

1704 and C01-1705) are not concurrently feasible. All PJM has done is make the confusing and

conclusory statement that “a deed or lease cannot convey an exclusive right to the same legal entity

twice, nor can it show conveyance to the same legal entity twice. Nor can such a document be

sufficient to demonstrate that both Projects are ‘concurrently feasible,’ as the Tariff requires.”43

This blanket assertion does not support PJM’s case. The lease conveyed site control to the LLC,

and the LLC delineated separate rights to each project. The data RWE submitted to PJM showed

these projects are concurrently feasible and neither the Deficiency Notice, the Withdrawal Notice,

nor the PJM Answer has or can make any factually supported claim that refutes the evidence in

the applications that show the projects are concurrently feasible.44

         Further, PJM claims a Shared Facilities Agreement is required.45 But the two projects do

not share interconnection facilities. Indeed, RWE made that very plain to PJM as the image below

from the C01-1705 application shows.

43       Id. at 20.

However, this Tariff Section is inapplicable because it applies only when “a Project Developer submits a New Service
Request with Site Control evidence utilizing the Site that is also the subject of Site Control in New Service Requests
submitted by other Project Developer’s.” Here, the same developer submitted both New Service Requests.
Regardless, C01-1705 meets the requirements in this section of the Tariff.

          Yet, again, even if the two projects were to share interconnection facilities, there would be

no need for a single legal entity – the same LLC – to have a Shared Facilities Agreement with

itself. That contract would be invalid because a contract requires two parties and consideration

between those parties. If PJM wants separate legal entities to own New Service Requests on the

same site, it should add that requirement to its Tariff;46 but it cannot use this post hoc justification

for the withdrawal of project C01-1705.

         Finally, if there was a site control deficiency – which there is not – Section 403(B)(1)(b)

of the PJM Tariff provides that a developer will be provided “10 Business Days to respond to

Transmission Provider’s deficiency determination.” PJM identified new site control deficiencies

on July 22, 2026, and now new site control claims in its Answer. It is beyond dispute that PJM

mismanaged its review of the C01-1075 application, treating it as an uprate even though the

application stated it was a New Service Request and then raising the need for a Shared Facilities

Agreement even though the application clearly stated no shared interconnection facilities are

needed. Had PJM undertaken a proper review of the application in the first place, it would have

known that C01-1705 is a New Service Request, not an uprate, and flagged its now-claimed

deficiencies in the June Deficiency Notice, which then would have afforded RWE the 10 business

 days to answer and cure, if needed, and resolve the alleged issues so the project could have

smoothly moved forward in Cycle 01 without the need for the Complaint. PJM’s mismanagement,

however, deprived RWE of the 10 business-day cure period – which serves both the customer and

PJM – and PJM withdrew C01-1705 from Cycle 01 on faulty information and bases less than 10

business days after its July 22, 2026, email.47

       For all these reasons, PJM had no Tariff basis to withdraw Project C01-1705 from Cycle

01, and doing so violated the PJM Tariff and the filed rate doctrine.

       C.      Reinstatement of the Projects Would Not Significantly Delay Cycle 01

       PJM fearmongers that reinstating the Projects would delay the start of Phase I of Cycle 01

by up to two months. 48 This is not a reason to deny the Complaint and refuse to reinstate the

Projects into Cycle 01. To the extent any delay were to occur, as the facts show, PJM would not

be in this position if it did not mismanage an initial application, provide inconsistent directions,

provide direction that was not rooted in its Tariff and Manuals and render inconsistent results for

identical modeling processes that led to the acceptance of many RWE projects and the withdrawal

of the five Projects at issue in this Complaint. Moreover, delay in processing the queue does not

trump following the FPA requirements and the filed rate doctrine. If delay is the outcome to ensure

the FPA and Court precedent are followed, then that is the right outcome. The FPA is a customer

protection statute and the Commission will be acting within that FPA mandate to grant the

Complaint.

       Further, PJM overstates the claimed delay. It would take PJM only a few days to add the

Projects to its models and commence the study process.



47     Id.
48     PJM Answer at 24-26.
                                                  16
        PJM points to PJM Manual 14H, Section 2.9 and states that “at least 30 days prior to

initiating Phase I of the Cycle, PJM will post the Phase I base case data for review. Specifically,

the PSSE summer peak base case model for the Cycle will be available.” Further, Tariff Section

403(B)(4) states that during “the Application Review Phase, and at least 30 days prior to initiating

Phase I of the Cycle, Transmission Provider will post the Phase I Base Case data for review, subject

to CEII protocols.” However, there is no Tariff requirement that this model cannot change over

those 30 days. In fact, PJM has posted additional models and made changes to the model since it

was posted.

       On August 28, 2026, PJM posted the Cycle 01 preliminary Phase I summer peak load flow

model and said it would commence Cycle 01 Phase I analysis on September 28, 2026, the first

business day at least 30 days following the preliminary model posting date.49 On September 4,

2026, PJM posted the Cycle 01 preliminary Phase I light load flow model and an updated summer

peak case.50 The update to the summer peak case made some minor corrections to files and, more

importantly, it added Project C01-2223 project, which was not in the initial case.51 When PJM

added that new project, it did not restart the 30-day clock because the Tariff does not require it.

On September 11, 2026, PJM then posted a new model, the Cycle 1 preliminary Phase 1 winter

peak load flow model, and the Phase I analysis was still set to begin on September 28, 2026.52

Further, PJM has recognized that projects could withdraw from Cycle 01 before September 28,

2026, changing the models further.53 Moreover, any impact on future Cycles is speculative at best



49     8/28/26 Email from PJM (Attachment W).
50     9/4/26 Email from PJM (Attachment X).
51     Id.
52     9/11/26 Email from PJM (Attachment Y).
53     9/25/26 Email from PJM (Attachment Z).
                                                17
     because PJM is evaluating an entirely new process that would integrate generation interconnection,

    load integration, and transmission planning that could eliminate Cycle 02 as PJM stated in the PJM

    Co-Located Load Order Workshop on September 16, 2026. Thus, there is no reason that adding

    the Projects will cause months of delay, and the minimal delay that would occur cannot trump

    ensuring that the FPA and Tariff are followed and customers are protected.

    III.   CONCLUSION

           For the foregoing reasons, RWE respectfully requests that the Commission grant this

    Motion for Leave to Answer, accept this Answer into the record of this proceeding, and grant the

    relief requested in the Complaint.

                                         Respectfully submitted,

                                         /s/ Bruce A. Grabow

                           AFFIDAVIT OF KARTHIK MEKALA

       1.     My name is Karthik Mekala. I am a Director of Transmission Analysis, U.S. East,

at RWE Americas, LLC (“RWE”). RWE is an electric generation developing company located at

353 N. Clark Street, Floor 30 in Chicago, Illinois. A large portion of my job involves leading

transmission analysis for energy projects across multiple regions in the Eastern Interconnection,

ensuring that each project’s grid impact, upgrade costs and deliverability results are accurately

assessed. This includes interpreting complex study results, engaging with independent system

operators (“ISOs”) and regional transmission organizations (“RTOs”), like PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C. (“PJM”) and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and strategically positioning

projects for cost-effective and timely interconnection.    I also guide cross-functional teams,

coordinate with developers, consultants, and regulatory teams, and contribute to policy and

regulatory discussions that shape future transmission planning and interconnection reform. I have

been involved extensively in submitting applications and analyzing system impact studies across

multiple ISOs/RTOs. I have previously filed an affidavit before the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission in connection with Docket No. ER25-712 and Docket No. EL26-7.
        2.      With this Affidavit, I verify, to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief,

the factual information summarized in Attachments K through S that RWE submitted with the

Complaint in this proceeding. The Attachments include information developed by me and my

colleagues based on the project records and materials reasonably available to us, and I personally

oversaw the development of Attachments K through S. References to RWE having “provided

technical justification” include, as applicable, revised model packages, benchmark reports,

calculations, technical data, supporting documentation, and written explanations submitted to

PJM. The deficiency notice tables compare PJM’s treatment of the same or materially similar

technical issues across RWE’s Cycle 01 projects, including BESS projects using the same inverter

model, submitted P-Q curve, and PSS®E version, where PJM reached different conclusions for

the projects at issue in this Complaint.

       3.      This completes my affidavit.

                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                 )
        Respondent                               )
                                                 )


                                        VERIFICATION

       I, Karthik Mekala, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of

America that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief.


                                              /s Karthik Mekala
                                              Karthik Mekala
September 28, 2026
